planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in spring once the soil is workable, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kuganskaya is self-fertile and its exceptional winter hardiness lets it succeed in colder gardens where standard Smyrna-type quince suffer dieback.

directions: Kuganskaya is a quince selection out of southern Russia bred specifically for cold tolerance well beyond what most quince cultivars can survive, making it a rare option for growers in colder climates who still want a true quince harvest. The tree forms a compact, rounded small tree and blooms with the pale pink flowers typical of the species before setting medium-sized, golden-yellow, strongly aromatic fruit that ripens in the second half of fall. Like other quince, the raw flesh is dense and astringent and must be cooked to soften into the rosy, honeyed preserves, paste, and jelly the fruit is prized for. It is self-fertile and needs no second tree, and an open, well-pruned canopy helps guard against fire blight in humid regions.

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Iranian medlar is self-fertile and, like other medlar selections, needs no second tree to set a full crop.

directions: Iranian is a large-fruited medlar accession originating from Persia, held in European fruit collections as a distinct genotype valued for fruit size and flavor rivaling the best Western European cultivars. The small, gnarled tree carries the same showy white spring flowers and open, twisting habit typical of the species, followed by hard, russet-brown fruit that must be bletted after harvest, stored in a cool spot for several weeks past the first frosts until it softens and darkens into a rich, spiced, wine-like pulp. It tolerates poor soils and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, fruiting best on a sheltered, sunny site where the spring blossom escapes late frosts. Harvest once fruit has colored fully and the calyx end has opened, then set aside to blet before eating fresh or cooking into preserves.

common_name: Rosie Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Purple Basil for Containers)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50F; Rosie holds a tight, uniform mounded habit that suits pots and small beds.

directions: Sow indoors and transplant after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow directly in containers. A 2022 All-America Selections winner, Rosie produces small, glossy, deep-purple leaves on a dense, compact, uniform mound that holds its color and shape more consistently than older purple types like Dark Opal. Pinch flower spikes and harvest young leaves regularly for salads, garnishes, and vinegars to keep the plant bushy and productive.

common_name: Everleaf Genovese Basil (Non-Flowering Extended-Harvest Genovese Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; the non-flowering habit means fewer resows are needed through summer.

directions: The original release in the Everleaf breeding series that later added Everleaf Thai Towers and Everleaf Emerald Towers, this classic Genovese-flavored basil is bred for a sterile, non-flowering habit so plants keep channeling energy into leaf production instead of seed set. The upright, well-branched plants hold sweet, glossy dark-green leaves in classic pesto flavor for weeks longer than standard Genovese types before quality declines. Harvest by cutting stem tips regularly to encourage continued branching.

common_name: Green Ruffles Basil (Frilled Lettuce-Leaf Ornamental-Culinary Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun; the large ruffled leaves bruise easily so handle transplants gently.

directions: Sow indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. The green-leaved companion to Purple Ruffles basil, this heirloom-type ornamental basil produces large, deeply crinkled and fringed lettuce-leaf-shaped foliage with sweet, mild classic basil flavor good for salads and pesto. Its dramatic ruffled texture also makes it a popular edible-ornamental for borders and containers; pinch flower spikes to prolong leaf production.

common_name: Aroma 2 Basil (Highly Aromatic Disease-Tolerant Genovese-Type Hybrid Basil)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 50F.

directions: Sow indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. This vigorous hybrid Genovese-type basil was bred for exceptionally strong, sweet basil aroma and flavor along with improved vigor and tolerance to common basil diseases compared to open-pollinated Genovese strains. Large, glossy dark-green leaves hold up well through the season for continuous cutting; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep plants leafy and productive for pesto and fresh use.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike many low echeverias, coccinea develops visible branching stems over time.

directions: Plant in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun. Coccinea is a shrubby, semi-sprawling species with branched stems that carry rosettes of blue-green leaves densely covered in fine silver hairs, the margins often flushing red in strong light. Its Latin name refers to the vivid scarlet, tubular flowers that rise on tall stalks above the foliage. Let soil dry completely between waterings and protect from hard frost and winter wet.

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained soil; give at least 4-5 hours of direct sun daily to bring out the coppery leaf color.

directions: Grow in bright, direct sun in gritty, sharply drained soil. Copper Rose is a freely branching Mexican species with slender naked stems topped by rosettes of glossy, dark green leaves that flush a rich coppery-red under strong sun and cool weather. Water thoroughly then let the soil dry out completely before watering again, and never let water sit in the crown of the rosette. It offsets readily along its stems to form a spreading, multi-headed clump over time.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in free-draining succulent mix; feed with a diluted liquid seaweed feed every 2 weeks during the main spring-summer growing season for best form and color.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in gritty, free-draining soil, avoiding harsh full afternoon sun in summer. Native to Mexico and nicknamed the Mexican firecracker, this compact species forms rosettes of green leaves covered in small whitish hairs that help shield the foliage from intense light. It is a branching succulent that offsets readily, forming small clusters. Stop watering during frosty conditions and keep it dry for several months over winter.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in mineral, well-drained soil; keep water out of the rosette center and give a cool, bright exposure rather than the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in well-draining mineral soil in cool full to part-day sun. This compact variety forms a solitary rosette of thick, convex, blue-green leaves blushed pink toward their dark red-tipped points, native to gypsum hills near Zaragoza in Nuevo Leon, Mexico. In late winter and early spring it produces long-lasting, urn-shaped flowers that are pink outside and yellow within. Water only occasionally, letting the mix dry fully between waterings, and keep the crown dry to prevent rot.

planting.note: Root offsets or cuttings in spring in well-drained soil; give full sun for the most vivid reddish-purple leaf margins.

directions: Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, watering only occasionally. Collected from pine-oak woodlands near Zimapan, Hidalgo, Mexico at elevation, this species forms an open rosette on short, stout stems of narrow, lightly fuzzy bright green leaves edged in reddish-purple. In summer it sends up flowering stalks bearing unusual two-toned blooms, with bluish-violet buds opening to coral-to-red petals tipped with yellow stamens. Protect from hard frost, as its cold hardiness has not been well established.

planting.note: Separate rosette offsets in spring and plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; water only occasionally once established.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, sharply drained soil. Native to the Barranca de Tolantongo region of Hidalgo, Mexico, this stemless, evergreen species offsets freely into clusters of rosettes made up of deltoid, pointed leaves in an unusual brownish-purple color. Large apricot-pink flowers rise well above the foliage on tall, three-branched flowering stems in summer, the trait that gives the species its name. It tolerates light frost down to the mid-20s Fahrenheit but appreciates winter protection from prolonged wet.

common_name: Juarez Hen and Chicks (Blue-Green Undulating-Leaf Succulent)

planting.note: Separate offsets in spring and plant in well-drained soil in cool sun to light shade; water sparingly and let dry fully between waterings.

directions: Grow in cool sun to light shade in well-drained soil, watering sparingly to occasionally. Native to Oaxaca, Mexico, this evergreen species forms solitary or clustered rosettes to about 10 inches wide of upright, slightly arching, blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves with gently undulating margins and a red-outlined blunt tip. Apricot-pink flowers appear on stalks above the foliage in summer. It has proven cold-hardy to the mid-20s Fahrenheit in cultivation, tolerating occasional light frost better than many echeverias.

planting.note: Handle very gently when planting divisions or fallen leaves, as this species drops leaves at the slightest touch; use gritty, well-drained soil in partial sun.

directions: Grow in bright but filtered light in gritty, well-drained soil, watering only occasionally. This rare, glabrous species from tropical deciduous canyon forest in Veracruz, Mexico forms a nearly stemless, flattened solitary rosette only an inch or two tall and about 4 inches wide, with spatulate leaves in reddish-purple to pinkish-grey-violet outlined in a thin cream margin. Its name references how easily the leaves detach from the rosette, so handle it with care. Pale orange flowers appear on slender, unbranched stalks from late winter into spring.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

common_name: Mauna Loa Echeveria (Large Ruffled Gibbiflora Hybrid)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; keep water out of the rosette to prevent rot.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, gritty soil. A showy Echeveria gibbiflora hybrid bred by succulent breeder Dick Wright, Mauna Loa grows on a stout stem into a large rosette of broad, crinkled, ruffled leaves marked with pronounced warty carunculations, the older leaves deepening to a rich red. Nodding orange-pink flowers appear on tall, branched stalks in fall. Water deeply then allow the soil to dry out completely, and never let water pool in the center of the rosette.

common_name: Big Red Echeveria (Large Rose-Red Margined Rosette Hybrid)

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings, or plant offsets, in spring in gritty cactus-and-succulent mix in full sun for the strongest red coloring.

directions: Plant in well-drained cactus and succulent mix with 50-70% mineral grit, in full sun. This large hybrid forms a solitary rosette 12 to 18 inches across of broad, thick, triangular leaves that crinkle along the margins and curl toward the center; leaves emerge green with red margins that darken from the tip downward until the entire leaf turns a deep rose-red, most intense in strong sun and cool seasons. Water deeply, then let the soil dry out completely before watering again, and propagate easily from offsets or leaf and stem cuttings.

common_name: Sunstruck False Sunflower (Compact Cream-and-Green Variegated Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Sunstruck holds its dense, mounded shape and heaviest variegation with a full day of direct light.

directions: Sunstruck is a Walters Gardens introduction bred to bring the appeal of variegated false sunflower down to a much smaller scale than older marbled-leaf selections, forming a dense, low mound of green foliage streaked with creamy white beneath a steady crop of two-inch, single, golden-yellow daisy flowers. It begins blooming earlier in the season than many heliopsis and continues from early summer into fall, drawing bees and butterflies throughout. The compact habit needs no staking and fits well at the front of a border, in a mixed container, or massed as a foliage accent even when not in flower. Grow in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil; divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bit of Honey False Sunflower (Variegated Semi-Double Gold Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil; Bit of Honey blooms most heavily and holds its bushy, upright habit best in full sun.

directions: Bit of Honey pairs white foliage boldly veined in deep green with unusually large, three-to-three-and-a-half-inch, semi-double golden-yellow flowers carrying multiple rows of petals around a gold cone, a combination not found in older variegated heliopsis selections. It forms a dense, upright, bushy clump noticeably more compact than 'Tuscan Sun' and similar older cultivars, making it easier to place in a mixed border without staking. Blooms open in midsummer and continue into early fall, attracting bees and butterflies steadily. Grow in full sun for the strongest variegation and flower count, though it tolerates part shade; average, evenly moist, well-drained soil suits it best, and clumps can be divided in spring every three to four years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Burning Hearts False Sunflower (Dark-Stemmed Red-Centered Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Burning Hearts carries its dark stems most uprightly with a full day of direct light.

directions: Burning Hearts contrasts near-black purple stems and foliage with two-to-three-inch daisy flowers whose yellow-orange rays surround a glowing red-orange to brownish-yellow center cone, a two-tone effect distinct from the all-red-orange, no-yellow blooms of the related 'Bleeding Hearts' selection. Stiff, dark stems stand upright through the summer without staking under normal conditions, though plants in too much shade may need support. It flowers from midsummer through the season, drawing butterflies and other pollinators, and tolerates a wide range of soils from poor and dry to average clay once established. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering, and divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; this old-fashioned umbellifer prefers cool conditions and can also be fall-sown in mild climates for an earlier, longer-stemmed spring crop.

directions: Sow directly into average, well-drained soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 6-9 inches apart, since bupleurum resents root disturbance from transplanting. Round, perfoliate blue-green leaves clasp the branching stems, which give rise to flat clusters of tiny lime-green flowers backed by leafy chartreuse bracts, an old cottage-garden filler once grown for dye and medicine and now prized by florists for its airy texture. Plants bolt and fade once summer heat sets in, so succession sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall stems in milder regions. Cut when bracts have fully colored for the best vase life, which can exceed two weeks.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for earliest, largest seed heads, or direct sow after frost danger passes; a head start lengthens the harvest window for dried stems.

directions: Transplant or direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 8-12 inches apart to support the tall, wiry stems. 'Ping Pong' was selected from the species for its exceptionally large, perfectly round drumstick seedheads, straw-colored globes patterned with a faint starburst that dry beautifully and hold their shape for months in arrangements. Pale lavender-blue pincushion flowers appear first and can be cut fresh, but most growers let blooms mature fully on the stem before harvesting the papery seed balls for drying. Cut and hang stems upside down in a dark, airy space as soon as the heads firm up and lose their green color for the sturdiest dried result.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers
